primary_claim: A GPT-2 crosscoder regularized with a sentence-level graph-based structured prior achieves reconstruction fidelity comparable to a vanilla L1-sparse crosscoder (R²=0.935 vs 0.940) while better preserving external semantic-neighborhood structure (higher Precision@64), whereas a crosscoder with an isotropic Gaussian prior underperforms substantially on both fidelity and sparsity; Ladder SAE results are still pending

effect.value: Graph crosscoder R²=0.9347 (Dead 84.72%) vs Vanilla R²=0.9401 (Dead 92.83%) vs Gaussian-iso R²=0.6870 (Dead 13.16%); Graph Precision@64=0.01340 vs Vanilla 0.01289

contradicts_or_qualifies: their own Part I suggestion that an isotropic Gaussian prior is an easier starting point; this post finds it underperforms both fidelity and sparsity compared to structured priors
stated_future_work: build better similarity graphs: symmetric kNN, degree-normalized Laplacian, combine token+sentence+category graphs for multi-scale structure
graph-aware training: edge sampling, periodic neighbor refresh, k ablations
test constraint combinations: graph penalty plus small L1 to probe the reconstruction-sparsity Pareto frontier
variational parity: compare a Gaussian-structured KL prior to the deterministic Graph penalty at matched compute
scale to larger LMs/datasets, add parent-to-child probes across layers, and run the planned Ladder SAE experiments
limitations_stated: Ladder SAE experimental results are still pending; only crosscoder results are reported so far
Gaussian-iso crosscoder substantially underperforms on fidelity and sparsity because an isotropic prior ignores empirical neighborhood adjacency
graph construction uses asymmetric kNN graphs (FAISS) without graph-aware batching, likely explaining Vanilla's marginally higher NDCG
Graph crosscoder does not clearly outperform Vanilla on raw reconstruction fidelity/sparsity, only on local neighborhood precision
quote: Vanilla and Graph achieve comparable and high fidelity R2 (0.940 vs 0.935) with low MSE, while Gaussian-iso lags on both fidelity and sparsity.
